title: Pacing in real races
goal: Apply pacing evidence to the marathon, the cycling time trial, triathlon and ultras, and judge what race data can and can't show.

steps.title: Marathons: most runners slow down
steps.text:
Big race data show how amateurs pace. Across 14 US marathons and 91,929 finishes, the second half was on average 15.6% slower than the first for men and 11.7% for women [[c:deaner-slow]]. Women's odds of keeping their pace (slowing less than 10%) were 1.46 times men's. Slower finishers slowed more, and more racing experience went with less slowing.

To measure your own pacing, compare the two halves' [split times](g:split-time):

**pace change (%) = (second-half time − first-half time) ÷ first-half time × 100**

A positive number means you slowed (a [positive](g:positive-pacing) split); a negative one means you sped up.

claims.text: In 91,929 US marathon performances, second-half pace slowed by 15.6% in men and 11.7% in women; women were more likely to maintain pace.

evidence.quote: The mean change in pace was 15.6% and 11.7% for men and women, respectively (P < 0.0001).
The odds for women were 1.46 (95% confidence interval, 1.41-1.50; P < 0.0001) times higher than men to maintain the pace

steps.title: How much did she slow?
steps.problem: A runner passes halfway in 1:45:00 and finishes in 3:45:00. What is her pace change?
steps: Times in minutes: halfway 105 min, finish 225 min.
Positive: she slowed by 14.3%, between the average for women and for men in the big US data set.

steps.title: Hitting the wall
steps.text:
[Hitting the wall](g:hitting-the-wall) is a large, lasting slowdown late in a marathon, typically after about 32 km (20 miles), usually because the body's energy stores run low [[c:wall-def]]. In more than 4 million race records, 28% of men and 17% of women hit it, and it was more common in the 3 years either side of a runner's personal best [[c:wall-rate]].

Pace and fuel are linked: running faster burns [glycogen](g:glycogen) faster, and muscles hold only about 400 g (*Fatigue in long efforts*). So the two defences are a start no faster than goal pace and carbohydrate taken during the race (the fueling module covers how much).

claims.text: Hitting the wall is a significant late-race slowdown in the marathon, typically after 20 miles and usually from depleted energy stores.

evidence.quote: The phenomenon known as hitting the wall (HTW) refers to the iconic hazard of the marathon distance, in which runners experience a significant slowing of pace late in the race, typically after the 20-mile mark, and usually because of a depletion of the body's energy stores.

claims.text: In over 4 million records, 28% of male and 17% of female recreational marathoners hit the wall; slowdowns were more frequent around a personal best.

evidence.quote: We find male runners more likely to slow significantly (hit the wall) than female runners; 28% of male runners hit the wall compared with 17% of female runners
Such slowdowns are more frequent in the 3 years immediately before and after a recent personal-best (PB) time

steps.title: The cycling time trial
steps.text:
On a flat course in steady conditions, a time trial longer than about 10 min is best ridden at [even](g:even-pacing) power, yet even experienced riders tend to start too hard [[c:tt-start]]. With hills or changing wind, vary power with the course: harder uphill and into the wind (*Pacing by physiology*).

Pace by power, not by feel or heart rate. Planned changes of about ±5% are too small for RPE or heart rate to track reliably [[c:tt-power]], and heart rate also creeps up over a long ride ([cardiovascular drift](g:cardiovascular-drift)).

For a flat 40 km: hold target power from the start even though it feels easy, and spend what's left in the last few kilometres.

claims.text: Even experienced cyclists tend to choose too high a power at the start of a longer time trial.

evidence.quote: It seems that even experienced cyclists naturally select a supraoptimal work rate at the start of a longer TT.

claims.text: Variable pacing is best monitored with power meters, because heart rate and perceived effort are insensitive to small changes in power.

evidence.quote: This strategy would be best monitored with 'power-measuring devices' rather than heart rate or subjective feelings as the sensitivity of these variables to small but meaningful changes in power during a race is low.

steps.title: Triathlon: ride for the run
steps.text:
The bike leg sets up the run. 10 triathletes ran 5 km faster after a 20 km ride at constant power (1118 s) than after rides of the same average at self-chosen (1134 s) or varying power (1168 s) [[c:bernard-even]]. 12 triathletes ran 9.3 km 42 s slower after an hour of highly variable cycling (40–140% of [maximal aerobic power](g:maximal-aerobic-power)) than after steady cycling at the same average [[c:etx-var]].

Elite draft-legal races differ. [Drafting](g:drafting) saves energy on the bike for the run [[c:draft-save]], and power swings with the pack: in a World Cup race, 17% of the bike leg was above maximal aerobic power [[c:bernard-wc]].

claims.text: A 5 km run was faster after constant-power cycling than after self-paced or variable-power cycling of the same average.

evidence.quote: Running performance was significantly improved after CI ride (1118 +/- 72 s) compared to those after FCI ride (1134 +/- 64 s) or VI ride (1168 +/- 73 s) despite similar metabolic responses and performances reported during the three cycling bouts.

claims.text: A 9.3 km run was 42 s slower after highly variable cycling than after constant cycling at the same mean power.

evidence.quote: The 9.3-km run time was 42 ± 37 s slower (mean ± 90% confidence limits [CL]) after VAR (35:32 ± 3:18 min:s, mean ± SD) compared with CON cycling (34:50 ± 2:49 min:s).

claims.text: Drafting on the bike saves energy and improves the following run.

evidence.quote: These results showed that drafting allows triathletes to save significantly on energy during the bike leg of a triathlon and creates the conditions for an improved running performance, with higher benefits for the strong runners.

claims.text: In a Triathlon World Cup bike leg, 17% of the time was spent above maximal aerobic power.

evidence.quote: The distribution of time was 51 +/- 9% for zone 1, 17 +/- 6% for zone 2, 15 +/- 3% for zone 3, and 17 +/- 6% was performed at workloads higher than MAP (zone 4).

debate.question: Does variable bike power hurt the run that follows?

sides.position: Yes: 5 km and 9.3 km run times were slower after variable than after constant cycling at the same average power.
Not always: after 30 min of cycling alternating ±20% every 5 min, a high-intensity run to exhaustion lasted longer than after constant cycling.

steps.title: Ultras: start slower than you think
steps.text:
In ultras almost everyone slows, but by how much differs. In a 100 km race that included the World Masters Championships, the fastest quarter of finishers ran the first 30 km at lower speeds *relative to their own average* than everyone else, and were relatively faster later; women started relatively slower and finished relatively faster than men [[c:renfree-ultra]]. In 13,829 finishes of the Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc (UTMB), a steadier pace went with faster finishing times [[c:suter-utmb]].

Careful with cause and effect: these are observational data. Fitter, more experienced runners may pace evenly *because* they are strong, rather than being fast because they pace evenly.

claims.text: In a 100 km race, the fastest quarter of finishers ran at lower relative speeds early; women started relatively slower and finished faster than men.

evidence.quote: Group 1 ran at significantly lower relative speeds than all other groups in the first three 10-km segments (all P < 0.01)
Females showed lower relative starting speeds and higher finishing speeds than males.

claims.text: Across 13,829 UTMB results, even pacing correlated with faster finishing times.

evidence.quote: Even pacing throughout the UTMB® correlated with faster finishing times.

points: Most amateur marathoners slow: about 16% (men) and 12% (women) in the second half. Pace change % = (second half − first half) ÷ first half × 100.
Hitting the wall (about 28% of men, 17% of women) is a late collapse, usually from low energy stores: don't start faster than goal pace, and fuel.
Time trials: even power on flat, steady courses; vary with hills and wind; pace by power, because RPE and heart rate miss ±5% changes.
Triathlon: steady bike power usually gives the faster run, though one study disagrees; elite draft-legal racing is variable by nature.
Ultras: the best finishers start relatively slower. Race data are observational, so they show links, not causes.

variants.stem: A runner passes halfway in 1:50:00 and finishes in 3:52:00. What is his pace change?

options.text: 10.9% slower
9.8% slower
options.why: This divides by the second-half time (12 ÷ 122). Divide by the first half.

options.text: 5.2% slower
options.why: This divides by the finish time (12 ÷ 232). Divide by the first half.

options.text: 10.9% faster
options.why: Right size, wrong sign: the second half took longer, so he slowed.

variants.solution: Second half = 232 − 110 = 122 min. Pace change = (122 − 110) ÷ 110 × 100 = 10.9%: a positive split, he slowed.

variants.stem: A runner passes halfway in 1:25:00 and finishes in 2:58:00. What is her pace change?

options.text: 9.4% slower
options.why: Right: second half 93 min; (93 − 85) ÷ 85 × 100 = 9.4%.

options.text: 8.6% slower
options.why: This divides by the second-half time (8 ÷ 93). Divide by the first half.

options.text: 4.5% slower
options.why: This divides by the finish time (8 ÷ 178). Divide by the first half.

options.text: 9.4% faster
options.why: Right size, wrong sign: the second half took longer, so she slowed.

variants.solution: Second half = 178 − 85 = 93 min. Pace change = (93 − 85) ÷ 85 × 100 = 9.4%: she slowed, but under 10%, so she 'kept the pace' by Deaner's definition.

variants.stem: In the marathon of an Ironman, a triathlete passes halfway in 1:40:00 and finishes the run in 3:35:00. What is his pace change?

options.text: 15.0% slower
13.0% slower
options.why: This divides by the second-half time (15 ÷ 115). Divide by the first half.

options.text: 7.0% slower
options.why: This divides by the run time (15 ÷ 215). Divide by the first half.

options.text: 15.0% faster
options.why: Right size, wrong sign: the second half took longer, so he slowed.

variants.stem: In large marathon data sets, who tends to slow most in the second half?

options.text: Men, and slower finishers
options.why: Right: men slowed more than women in all 14 races, and slower finishers slowed more.

options.text: Women, because their VO2max is lower
options.why: Women slowed less, and the gap shrank but remained after adjusting women's times for men's higher VO2max.

options.text: The fastest finishers, who start most aggressively
options.why: Faster finishers slowed less, not more.

options.text: Nobody in particular: everyone slows by about the same amount
options.why: Slowing differed clearly by sex, finish time and experience.

variants.stem: A recreational runner holds 5:00 per km to 30 km, then over a few kilometres slows to 7:00 per km and stays there. She took no carbohydrate during the race. What is the most likely cause, and the best prevention?

options.text: Low glycogen: start no faster than goal pace and take carbohydrate during the race
options.why: Right: a sudden, lasting late slowdown is the classic wall, usually from depleted energy stores.

options.text: Lactic acid build-up: stretch more and warm up longer before the race
options.why: Lactate doesn't cause a late, lasting collapse at marathon pace, and stretching doesn't change fuel.

options.text: Low VO2max: add more sprint intervals to her training
options.why: Her pace was fine for 30 km; the collapse came from fuel, not from aerobic capacity.

options.text: Worn-out shoes: switch to a softer, more cushioned pair
options.why: Shoes don't explain a sudden, lasting slowdown after 30 km without fuel.

variants.stem: A cyclist plans to ride 5% above her average power into a headwind and 5% below it with the tailwind. What should she pace by?

options.text: A power meter
options.why: Right: power shows a 5% change at once and exactly.

options.text: Heart rate
options.why: Heart rate responds too little to small changes of power, and drifts upward over long rides.

options.text: How hard it feels (RPE)
options.why: RPE is too insensitive to small but meaningful changes in power.

options.text: Speed
options.why: Speed changes with the wind: the same power is slower into a headwind, so speed can't show effort.

variants.stem: A rider has a flat 40 km time trial on a still day. Which plan does the evidence support?

options.text: Hold target power from the start, resisting the urge to go harder early
options.why: Right: even power is optimal here, and the usual mistake is a start that is too hard.

options.text: Start about 15% above target to bank time while fresh
options.why: Riders who start well above average lose more time later than they bank.

options.text: Ride the first half easy and the second half hard
options.why: A slow first half loses time that a hard second half can't recover in steady conditions.

options.text: Vary power by ±10% every kilometre to spread the load
options.why: With no hills or wind, variation buys no time and costs extra effort.

variants.stem: An age-group triathlete in a non-drafting sprint race wants the fastest 5 km run after the 20 km bike. How should she spread her bike power?

options.text: As evenly as the course allows
options.why: Right: in two of three studies, runs were faster after constant than after variable or self-paced cycling.

options.text: In hard surges to drop rivals, recovering in between
options.why: Highly variable cycling slowed the following run by 42 s over 9.3 km.

options.text: Easy for the first half, very hard for the last 5 km
options.why: That is a large power swing at the worst moment, just before the run; if anything, an easy last 5 min of cycling was suggested to help the run.

options.text: Any way she likes: only average power matters
options.why: With the same average power, the run time still depended on the spread.

variants.stem: One study found variable bike power improved the following run; two found it made the run slower. What best explains the disagreement?

options.text: Different run tests and swing patterns, in small groups of 8–12 athletes
options.why: Right: one used a run to exhaustion after mild ±20% swings ending on an easy 5 min, the others run time trials after other patterns; small groups give wide uncertainty.

options.text: The study that found a benefit must contain a calculation error
options.why: Nothing suggests an error; different designs can give different answers.

options.text: Variable cycling always helps; the other two studies timed the runs wrongly
options.why: Run time trials are a valid measure; the disagreement comes from design.

options.text: Running after cycling can't be measured reliably in any study
options.why: All three measured runs; the question is what each design tests.

variants.stem: In a 100 km race, how did the fastest quarter of finishers pace compared with slower runners?

options.text: Relatively slower early, relatively faster late
options.why: Right: lower relative speeds in the first 30 km, higher later.

options.text: Faster early to bank time, then holding on
options.why: That was the pattern of the slowest group, which started relatively fast.

options.text: Exactly the same relative pattern as everyone else
options.why: The groups differed clearly in the first three 10 km segments.

options.text: All-out start, then walking the second half
options.why: All-out pacing suits efforts of seconds, not 100 km.

variants.stem: Even pacing went with faster UTMB finishing times across 13,829 results. A coach concludes: "Even pacing will make any runner faster." What is the main problem?

options.text: Race data can't show cause: fitter runners may simply pace more evenly
options.why: Right: a link in race data doesn't show that changing pacing changes the result.

options.text: 13,829 results are too few to show anything about pacing
options.why: That is a large sample; the problem is the design, not the size.

options.text: Mountain races are too hilly to be paced evenly by anyone
options.why: Runners do pace mountain races; the study measured how steady they were.

options.text: The data come only from women, so they don't apply to men
options.why: Most of the results were from men (12,681 of 13,829).
